note.note:
History:
- Main complaint: Chest tightness for approximately 3 hours.
- Symptom details:
  - Tightness in chest (not described as pain).
  - Mild shortness of breath, worse with exertion (e.g., walking up stairs); no shortness of breath at rest.
  - Wheeze and persistent cough (non-productive); cough slightly worse at night but present throughout the day.
  - Recent viral illness: cold last week with sore throat and runny nose, now improved except for ongoing cough.
  - No chest pain; unable to take a full breath at times.
  - No mention of hemoptysis, fever, or sputum production.
- Previous severe asthma exacerbation requiring hospitalization and intubation at age 16–17.
- No history of recent asthma exacerbations until this episode.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (diagnosed in childhood; last severe exacerbation in adolescence with hospitalization).
- Allergic rhinitis/hay fever.
- Dust allergy.
- Childhood eczema and milk protein allergy (no ongoing symptoms).
- No known drug allergies.
- Medications:
  - Salbutamol (Ventolin) inhaler—ran out and not used for 1 week (dose/route/frequency not documented).
  - Clenil Modulite (beclometasone steroid inhaler)—ran out and not used for 1 week (dose/route/frequency not documented).

Physical Examination:
- No physical exam performed (virtual consult).
- Denies shortness of breath at rest.
- No chest pain (tightness only).
- Able to walk on flat ground; slight increased shortness of breath on stairs.
- No reports of throat swelling, alertness not impaired.
- Not recorded: vital signs, oxygen saturation, respiratory rate.

Impression:
- Likely asthma exacerbation triggered by recent viral upper respiratory tract infection and omission of regular inhalers.
- Top DDx considerations also include:
  1. Asthma exacerbation (primary diagnosis; consistent with history and symptoms).
  2. Post-viral cough/bronchial hyperreactivity (less likely: presence of wheeze and tightness, plus asthma history, favors exacerbation).
  3. Allergic (non-infectious) asthma exacerbation (possible, but timeline after viral illness suggests infectious trigger).
- No evidence of alternate causes (e.g., pulmonary embolism) — low clinical suspicion.

Management Plan:
- Prescribed new courses of both Salbutamol (Ventolin) and Clenil Modulite inhalers.
- Prescribed a 5-day course of oral steroids (dose not specified), two tablets each morning.
- To be sent a new spacer device with instructions.
- Advised:
  - Use Clenil Modulite as maintenance and Ventolin as needed, especially if wheezy.
  - Seek medical attention if needing Salbutamol (Ventolin) more frequently than every three hours or if symptoms worsen (e.g., increased shortness of breath, chest tightness, or light-headedness).
  - Rest from work until improved (self-certify up to seven days).
  - Monitor for steroid side effects (e.g., mood changes, rash, nausea, headache, hyperglycemia); read medication leaflet for full details.

Patient Summary:
- Daniel, a 26-year-old with asthma and allergies, presented with chest tightness, cough, and wheeze following a recent cold and after running out of inhalers for one week. This is most compatible with an asthma exacerbation. He will start prescribed steroids, resume inhalers, and use a spacer with instructions provided.

Key Takeaways:
- Resume both Ventolin and Clenil inhalers as prescribed and use the spacer.
- Complete the steroid course as directed and be aware of possible side effects.
- Seek medical attention immediately for worsening symptoms or need for reliever inhaler more often than every 3 hours.

Next Steps:
- Obtain and begin new inhalers and spacer as soon as possible.
- Take prescribed oral steroids for 5 days.
- Rest until symptoms improve; self-certify off work if needed.
- Monitor symptoms; if condition deteriorates, seek prompt medical help.
- Follow up as necessary if symptoms do not resolve or worsen.
